blocks.html: Look at our flag. It has stripes and stars. Let's count them together!

blocks.name: cv-flag
blocks.cap: Point to each stripe and count: 1, 2, 3… all the way to 13.

blocks.html: Our flag has 13 stripes, red and white, and 50 white stars on a blue square.
Each part of the flag means something. The 13 stripes are for the 13 colonies that became our first states. The 50 stars are for the 50 states we have today: one star for each state.

blocks.name: cv-flag
blocks.cap: The first flags had 13 stars. When a new state joined, a star was added. The 50-star flag came in 1960.

blocks.html: Some people think there is one stripe for each state. Not so! There are only 13 stripes, for the first 13 colonies. The stars are for the states. A quick check: 50 states, 50 stars.
For the grown-up: Flag Day is June 14, the day in 1777 when Congress chose the first flag. Count the stars together in rows if your child is ready: the rows have 6 and 5 stars, taking turns.

sources.name: U.S. Code, Title 4, Sections 1 and 2: the flag has thirteen stripes and one star for each state, added on the July 4 after a state joins (summarized in our own words)
Library of Congress blog, "Whose broad stripes and bright stars" (2017)

blocks.html: This big bird is the bald eagle. It is our national bird, a bird that stands for the whole country.
The bald eagle is a symbol of strength and freedom. It lives only in North America.

Long ago, in 1782, leaders chose the eagle for the Great Seal of the United States, the country's official stamp. An eagle is strong, flies high and is free, and bald eagles live only in North America. In 2024 Congress made it our official national bird.

"Bald" makes some children think the eagle has no feathers on its head. It does! A grown-up bald eagle has a head covered in white feathers and a brown body. Long ago, "bald" could mean "white-headed."
For the grown-up: The Great Seal is on the back of a one-dollar bill. Look at one together and find the eagle: it holds an olive branch in one foot and arrows in the other.

sources.name: The Great Seal of the United States, adopted by Congress in 1782 (summarized in our own words)
Bald eagle made the official national bird by a law signed December 24, 2024 (news report)

blocks.html: This is the Liberty Bell. It is a very old bell in the city of Philadelphia. Can you find its crack?
The Liberty Bell is a symbol of freedom. "Liberty" means freedom.

blocks.name: cv-doc
blocks.cap: These words are on the bell. Tap the big word.

blocks.html: The bell was made in 1753 for the building where, years later, leaders signed the Declaration of Independence. Its words say to proclaim liberty, which means to tell everyone about freedom. People who worked to end slavery named it the Liberty Bell, and it became a symbol of freedom for everyone.
Some children think the bell still rings every day. It cracked long ago, so it is not rung anymore. It is kept safe where visitors can see it.

sources.name: National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park: The Liberty Bell

blocks.html: This tall statue stands on an island in New York Harbor. She is the Statue of Liberty.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France in 1886. She holds up a torch to welcome people.

France and the United States were friends, and the people of France sent the statue as a gift of friendship and freedom. Long ago, many families came to America on ships. When they sailed into New York Harbor, the statue was one of the first things they saw: her torch held high, as if to say "Welcome."
Is the statue painted green? No! She is made of thin sheets of copper, a metal that was shiny brown at first. Over many years of wind and rain, the copper turned green by itself.

blocks.name: cv-doc
blocks.cap: A poem on a plaque at the statue. The grown-up can read it aloud.

sources.name: Ben's Guide (U.S. Government Publishing Office): The Statue of Liberty
Emma Lazarus, "The New Colossus" (1883, public domain)

blocks.html: Our country has a special song called the national anthem. Its name is "The Star-Spangled Banner." "Banner" means flag.
Francis Scott Key wrote the words in 1814, after he saw our flag still flying over Fort McHenry.

In 1814 the United States and Britain were at war. All night, British ships fired at Fort McHenry in Baltimore. Francis Scott Key watched from a ship. When the sun came up, he saw the big flag still waving over the fort, so he knew the fort had not given up. He was so happy that he wrote a poem. The poem became a song, and in 1931 Congress made it our national anthem.

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.note: In the morning light, Key saw the flag still flying. The fort had held.

blocks.cap: The first verse. Tap the highlighted words.

blocks.name: cv-flag
blocks.cap: The flag Key saw had 15 stars and 15 stripes.

blocks.html: Some children think the anthem is as old as the country. Key wrote it in 1814, and it became the national anthem in 1931, more than 100 years later.
For the grown-up: When the anthem plays, people stand and face the flag; many put a right hand over the heart. The flag Key saw is kept at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.

sources.name: National Park Service, Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine: press kit
Francis Scott Key, "Defence of Fort M'Henry" (1814, public domain), first verse

blocks.html: Every country has a capital, the city where its leaders work. Our capital is Washington, D.C.
Congress meets in the Capitol, the building with the big dome. The President lives and works in the White House.

The city is named after George Washington, our first President. "D.C." stands for "District of Columbia." It is not part of any state, so it belongs to the whole country. It is also full of monuments that honor great Americans.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Washington, D.C., is near the East Coast, close to Philadelphia and New York.

blocks.html: Washington, D.C., and the state of Washington are two different places, far apart. The capital is on the East Coast; the state is on the West Coast, by the Pacific Ocean. And the Capitol (where Congress meets) is not the White House (where the President lives).

sources.name: U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 8, Clause 17: Congress governs the seat of government (National Archives)
Ben's Guide (U.S. Government Publishing Office)

blocks.html: A rule tells us what to do, or what not to do. We have rules at home, at school and on the playground. Let's find out why.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Rules are all around us: a traffic light, a stop sign, the rules of a classroom.

blocks.html: Rules help keep us safe, help us be fair and help us get along.

Think about a game with no rules. Everyone wants the ball at once, and nobody knows who wins. Rules like "take turns" make the game fair, so it is fun for everyone. A traffic light is a rule, too: red means stop and green means go, so cars and people do not bump into each other.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.why: The red light keeps cars and people from crashing.
Taking turns gives everyone a chance.

cards.text: Walk, do not run, in the hallway
cards.why: Walking keeps people from falling and bumping.

cards.text: Everyone gets one piece of cake
cards.why: The same for each person is fair.

blocks.cap: Tap a card, then tap the group where it fits. Some rules do both jobs!

blocks.html: Some children think rules are only there to get them in trouble. Ask: "What would happen without this rule?" Without "take turns," some children would never get a turn. Rules protect everyone, and that includes you.
For the grown-up: Make a short list of family rules together and talk about the reason for each one. Children follow rules more easily when they know why.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards, Civics, grades K-2 (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), D2.Civ.12.K-2: explain how rules and laws change society and how people change rules

blocks.html: You know that rules help us at home and at school. A law is a rule, too. It is a rule for everyone who lives in a town, a state or the whole country.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A stop sign shows a law. A judge decides questions about laws. Congress makes laws for the country in the Capitol.

blocks.html: A rule can be for one family or one class. A law is for everyone, and it is made by leaders the people choose.

A family can make its own rules, like "Bedtime is at eight." But a town needs rules that all its people share, like where cars must stop. So the people choose leaders, and the leaders write laws. A town makes town laws, a state makes state laws, and Congress makes laws for the whole country.

blocks.name: cv-sort

bins: A rule at home or school

cards.text: Raise your hand to talk in class
Do not take things from a store without paying

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: is it a home or school rule, or a law for everyone?

blocks.html: Some children think laws are only for children. Not so! Laws are for everyone: grown-ups, teachers, police officers and even the President. Nobody is above the law.
For the grown-up: Point out laws you see on a walk: speed limit signs, crosswalks, "no parking" signs. Ask who made each one: the town, the state or the country.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards, Civics, grades K-2 (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), D2.Civ.12.K-2
Ben's Guide to the U.S. Government (U.S. Government Publishing Office)

blocks.html: A community is a place where people live, work and play together. Many people have jobs that help the whole community. They are community helpers.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Tools of five helpers: a fire truck, a police badge, a doctor's stethoscope, a mail bag and a school.

blocks.html: Each helper has a special job. Firefighters put out fires. Police officers help keep people safe and help enforce the laws. Doctors and nurses help sick people get well. Teachers help us learn. Mail carriers bring letters and packages.

No one can do every job alone. A town works because many people each do one job well and share it with everyone. Farmers grow food, bus drivers take people places and librarians help us find books. When each helper does a part, the whole community is better off.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Drives a big red truck with a ladder

blocks.cap: Match what each helper does.

blocks.html: It is easy to name a helper by the uniform or the truck. The bigger question is: "What does this helper do for us?" A firefighter does not only ride a truck; a firefighter keeps people and homes safe from fire.
For the grown-up: Many helpers are volunteers. Point out helpers you meet during the day and thank them together.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards, Civics, grades K-2 (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), D2.Civ.2.K-2: explain how all people, not just official leaders, play important roles in a community

blocks.html: A leader helps a group make choices and get things done. In our country, the people choose many of their leaders. They do it by voting.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: People put their votes in a ballot box. Leaders we vote for work in places like the Capitol and the White House.

blocks.html: In a vote, each person gets one vote. We count all the votes, and the choice with the most votes wins.

Voting is fair because every vote counts the same. It does not matter who is the loudest or the tallest. Grown-up citizens vote for leaders: a mayor leads a town or city, a governor leads a state, and the President leads the whole country. In the United States, citizens can vote when they are 18.

blocks.title: Count the votes
blocks.q: A class votes for a class pet. Fish gets 7 votes. Hamster gets 9 votes. Which pet wins?
steps: Count the votes for each choice: fish 7, hamster 9.
Find the bigger number: 9 is more than 7.
The hamster has the most votes, so the hamster wins.

blocks.html: Some children think the winner is the choice they like best, or the side that shouts the loudest. A vote is decided by counting. Count every vote, and the most votes wins.
For the grown-up: Hold a family vote on a game or a snack. Let each person vote once, count out loud and talk about how the side that lost still gets a turn next time.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards, Civics, grades K-2 (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), D2.Civ.1.K-2 and D2.Civ.9.K-2: follow agreed-upon rules for discussions and making decisions
U.S. Constitution, Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971): citizens 18 years of age or older may vote (National Archives)

blocks.html: A citizen is a member of a country. A good citizen helps make the community a good place for everyone. You can be a good citizen right now!

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Good citizens help others, care for shared places like schools and parks, and, when they grow up, vote.

blocks.html: A good citizen follows the rules, tells the truth, helps others and takes care of shared places. Grown-up citizens also vote.

A community is shared by everyone in it. If each person picks up trash, waits in line and helps a neighbor, the park stays clean and people treat each other kindly. Community helpers do this as their job, but every citizen can help a little every day.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Throw trash in the trash can
Leave a mess at the park
Help a friend who fell down
Cut in front of the line

blocks.cap: Sort the cards.

blocks.html: Some children think "citizen" means only grown-ups or famous people. Anyone can practice good citizenship by sharing, helping and caring for the community. Voting waits until you are 18, but helping can start today.
For the grown-up: Pick one small act of good citizenship to do together this week, such as picking up litter in a park or making a card for a neighbor.

sources.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards, Civics, grades K-2 (National Council for the Social Studies, 2013), D2.Civ.2.K-2 and D2.Civ.7.K-2: apply civic virtues when participating in school settings

blocks.html: Every summer, on July 4, our country has a birthday party! There are parades, picnics, flags and fireworks. This day is called Independence Day, or the Fourth of July.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Fireworks, flags and the Declaration of Independence.

blocks.html: On July 4, 1776, leaders of the thirteen colonies adopted the Declaration of Independence. It said the colonies would be a new, free country: the United States of America.

Long ago, the colonies were ruled by Britain, far across the ocean. Many colonists wanted to rule themselves. So their leaders met in Philadelphia and wrote a letter to the world, the Declaration, saying "We are free and independent." That is why July 4 is the country's birthday. In 2026 the United States turned 250 years old!

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: From 1776 to 2026 is 250 years.

blocks.html: Some children think the Fourth of July is about fireworks, or the day a war ended. The fireworks are how we celebrate. The day remembers the Declaration. The war for independence went on for years after 1776.

For the grown-up: Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and approved the final words of the Declaration on July 4. That date is printed at the top of the document, so July 4 became the day we celebrate.

sources.name: The Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776 (National Archives transcription)
Grokipedia, "Independence Day (United States)" (the vote of July 2 and the adoption of July 4, 1776)
U.S. Code, Title 5, Section 6103: the legal public holidays (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: On Thanksgiving Day, families and friends share a meal and give thanks for the good things in their lives. It comes on the fourth Thursday in November.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Many families eat turkey, corn and pumpkin, foods first grown or found in the Americas.

blocks.html: Thanksgiving remembers a harvest feast in 1621, shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people. In 1863, President Abraham Lincoln asked the whole country to keep a day of thanks.

In 1621 the Pilgrims had their first harvest in their new home. The Wampanoag, who had lived on that land for a very long time, had helped them learn to grow corn. The Pilgrims and about 90 Wampanoag men feasted together for three days. Many years later, in 1863, Lincoln called for a national day of Thanksgiving, and Americans have kept it every year since.

Some children think the Pilgrims held Thanksgiving every year from 1621 on. The 1621 feast was a harvest celebration. Thanksgiving as a holiday for the whole country began in 1863, more than 200 years later.

events.label: Lincoln calls for a national Thanksgiving
A law sets the fourth Thursday in November

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Since 1970, some Wampanoag and other Native people have gathered in Plymouth on Thanksgiving for a National Day of Mourning, remembering what the coming of the colonists cost their nations. You can learn more in The Harvest Feast of 1621.

sources.name: Pilgrim Hall Museum, "The First Thanksgiving" (Winslow's and Bradford's accounts)
Grokipedia, "Thanksgiving (United States)" (Lincoln's proclamation of October 3, 1863; the fourth Thursday fixed by Congress in 1941)
Grokipedia, "National Day of Mourning (United States protest)" (first held in 1970)

blocks.html: In February we honor George Washington, our first President. The holiday's official name is Washington's Birthday. Many people call it Presidents' Day and honor all the Presidents.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Washington wore a three-cornered hat; Lincoln, also born in February, wore a tall stovepipe hat.

blocks.html: The holiday is on the third Monday in February. Washington was born on February 22, 1732.

Washington led the army that won independence and then became the first President, so the country wanted a day to remember him. For many years the holiday was on his real birthday, February 22. Starting in 1971, a law moved it to a Monday, so families could have a long weekend. Abraham Lincoln was born in February too (February 12), so many people honor both.
Some children think the holiday is on Washington's real birthday. Not anymore! The third Monday in February always lands between February 15 and February 21, so it never falls on the 22nd.

events.label: The holiday moves to the third Monday in February

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Look at a February calendar together. Find the Mondays, count to the third one and circle it. Then find February 22 and see how far apart they are this year. More about Washington is in George Washington.

sources.name: U.S. Code, Title 5, Section 6103: the legal public holidays (summarized in our own words)
Grokipedia, "Presidents' Day" (a federal holiday since 1879 and 1885; moved to the third Monday in February by the Uniform Monday Holiday Act, in effect from 1971)

blocks.html: In January we honor Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He was a minister and a leader who worked so that all people would be treated fairly, by peaceful means.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Dr. King helped lead a famous bus boycott. Many people spend his day helping others.

blocks.html: Martin Luther King Jr. Day is the third Monday in January, near his birthday, January 15. It was first kept across the country in 1986.

In Dr. King's time, unfair laws in many places kept Black Americans apart from others: in schools, on buses and at lunch counters. Dr. King gave speeches and led marches without fighting. He said people should be judged by who they are inside. Many people agreed, the laws changed, and the country chose a holiday to honor him. Many families spend the day helping others, as a "day of service."

Some children think Dr. King lived long ago, in Lincoln's time, or that he worked alone. He was born in 1929, about a hundred years after Lincoln, and he was one of many, many people who worked together for fair treatment.

events.label: Martin Luther King Jr. is born

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Dr. King was killed in 1968; you can choose when to share that. The law making the holiday was signed in 1983. His story continues in Rosa Parks and Dr. King.

sources.name: U.S. Code, Title 5, Section 6103: the legal public holidays (summarized in our own words)
Grokipedia, "Martin Luther King Jr. Day" (signed into law in 1983; first observed nationwide January 20, 1986)

blocks.html: Men and women in our armed forces serve the country. They are called service members, and people who have served are veterans. Two holidays honor them.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: On Memorial Day, people place wreaths, flowers and small flags at the graves of those who died in service.

blocks.html: Memorial Day (the last Monday in May) remembers service members who died serving our country. Veterans Day (November 11) thanks everyone who has served.

After the Civil War, families decorated soldiers' graves with spring flowers. This became Memorial Day. Veterans Day began as the day World War I fighting stopped: November 11, 1918, at 11 o'clock in the morning. Today Veterans Day thanks all veterans, and many of them are our neighbors, grandparents and friends.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Remembers those who died in service

blocks.cap: Which day is it?

blocks.html: The two days are easy to mix up. A memory trick: Memorial Day is for remembering those who died. Veterans Day is for thanking all veterans, and many of them are still alive.
For the grown-up: If you know a veteran, a thank-you card on November 11 is a good way to mark the day. Memorial Day began as "Decoration Day" in 1868.

blocks.html: Our country has eleven national holidays, and each one remembers something different. Let's meet a few more.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A broken chain stands for freedom; helping hands for workers; the flag for Flag Day.

blocks.html: Juneteenth (June 19) remembers the end of slavery. Labor Day (the first Monday in September) honors workers.

For a long time, many people in our country were enslaved: they were not free. On June 19, 1865, soldiers brought the news to Galveston, Texas, that the enslaved people there were free. People there celebrated, and in 2021 Juneteenth became a national holiday. Labor Day became a national holiday in 1894 to thank the people whose work builds the country.

head: Day
When
What it remembers
rows: Columbus's 1492 voyage; many places also mark Indigenous Peoples' Day
blocks.cap: Flag Day and Constitution Day are special days, but not days off.

blocks.html: Some children think every holiday is the same: a day off school. Each holiday has its own reason. Ask: "What does this day remember?"

For the grown-up: The eleven federal holidays are New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. Slavery is told more fully in Slavery and Freedom.

blocks.html: A calendar shows the days and months of the year. The year starts in January and ends in December. Let's put our holidays in order!

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Twelve months: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

blocks.html: To put holidays in order, find each holiday's month, then go through the months from January to December.

blocks.title: Which comes first?
blocks.q: Put these in order: Thanksgiving, Independence Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day.
steps: Find the months: Thanksgiving is in November. Independence Day is July 4. Martin Luther King Jr. Day is in January.
January comes first, then July, then November.
The order is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Independence Day, Thanksgiving.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Tap two to swap them, then Check. The months are there to help.

blocks.html: Some children start the year in September, when school begins, or put their favorite holiday first. The calendar year starts on January 1, New Year's Day.
For the grown-up: Hang a calendar where your child can see it and mark the holidays. Count how many months until the next one. Review the holidays in Juneteenth, Labor Day and Other Holidays.

blocks.html: Long, long before there was a United States, people already lived all across this land. They were the first peoples of America. Today we call them Native Americans, or American Indians.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Native peoples built a big city at Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, and homes in the cliffs at Mesa Verde. The Wampanoag lived near Plymouth.

blocks.html: Native Americans lived here for thousands of years before people from Europe came. There were hundreds of nations, each with its own language, leaders and way of life.

North America is very big. It has forests, deserts, mountains, grassy plains and long seacoasts. Each nation learned to live well in its own place. People by the ocean fished and built canoes. People on the plains followed the bison. Farmers grew corn and squash. So the nations were different from one another, the way the places were different.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Canoes, bison and corn were part of life for different nations.

blocks.html: Some children think all Native Americans lived the same way, or that they lived only long ago. There were (and are) many different nations, such as the Wampanoag, the Haudenosaunee, the Cherokee, the Lakota and the Navajo. Native nations are still here today.

For the grown-up: When you can, use a nation's own name (Wampanoag, Cherokee, Navajo) rather than "Indians" in general. Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, was the largest Native city north of Mexico; it was at its height about 1100.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Indigenous peoples of the Americas" (peoples, nations and languages)

blocks.html: The first peoples built their homes from what the land gave them: trees, bark, clay, animal skins and stone. Each kind of home fit its place.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A longhouse, a wigwam, a tipi, a pueblo and a plank house.

blocks.html: Different nations built different homes. A tipi could be packed up and moved. A longhouse, a pueblo and a plank house stayed in one place.

The Haudenosaunee built long longhouses of wood and bark, where many families lived together. In the eastern woods, peoples such as the Wampanoag made round wigwams of bent poles and bark. On the Great Plains, peoples who followed the bison lived in tipis of poles and buffalo hides, easy to move. In the dry Southwest, Pueblo peoples built homes of adobe, mud bricks dried in the sun, with ladders to the upper floors. By the Pacific, nations built big plank houses of cedar wood.
Some children think every Native family lived in a tipi. Tipis were homes for peoples who moved across the Great Plains. Most other nations built homes that stayed in one place.

blocks.name: cv-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the homes.

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Ask: "What is our home made of? Why do you think people built it that way?" Then compare it with the homes above.

blocks.html: Many Native nations were skilled farmers. Three plants grew so well together that the Haudenosaunee call them the Three Sisters.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Three Sisters: corn, beans and squash.

blocks.html: The Three Sisters are corn, beans and squash, planted together in one field. Each one helps the others.

The corn grows tall and straight, like a pole. The beans climb up the corn stalk and help feed the soil. The squash spreads big leaves over the ground, which shade the soil, keep it wet and keep weeds away. Working together, the three plants grow better than they would alone, and together they make a healthy meal.

blocks.name: cv-sort
blocks.cap: What does each sister do?

blocks.html: Some children think Native peoples only hunted. Many nations were farmers. Corn, potatoes, tomatoes, pumpkins and peppers were all first grown in the Americas. Today people all over the world eat them.
For the grown-up: At your next meal, look for foods first grown in the Americas: corn, potatoes, tomatoes, squash, pumpkins, peppers, many kinds of beans, and the cacao beans that make chocolate.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Three Sisters (agriculture)" (corn, beans and squash; prominent among the Haudenosaunee)

blocks.html: The first peoples are not only part of the past. Native nations are still here today, and Native Americans live in every state.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Drums, canoes and schools: many nations keep old traditions and teach their languages to children today.

blocks.html: Native nations have their own governments, leaders, languages and traditions. In 2026 the United States government lists 575 tribes.

Native nations governed themselves long before the United States began. Many of them still have their own councils and leaders, their own laws and courts, and their own flags. Some families live on land the nation holds, called a reservation; many others live in towns and cities. Children learn their nation's language and stories, and families gather for ceremonies, dances and powwows.

Some children talk about Native Americans only in the past, as if they were gone. Native nations live, govern themselves and keep their traditions today. Your classmates, neighbors or teachers may be members of one.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Native nations have their own governments
Native Americans lived only long ago
Many children learn their nation's language
Every Native family lives in a tipi

blocks.cap: True or not true?

blocks.html: For the grown-up: The Navajo Nation has the largest reservation, about 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. Look up which Native nations live, or once lived, where you live.

blocks.html: An explorer is a person who travels to learn about places that are new to them. Long ago, explorers from Europe sailed across the big Atlantic Ocean in wooden ships.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A sailing ship, a compass to find the way, and a globe.

blocks.html: Leif Erikson reached North America about the year 1000. Christopher Columbus sailed in 1492. After him, many more explorers came.

Leif Erikson came from the north, and his people built a small camp in what is now Canada, but they did not stay. Columbus sailed for the king and queen of Spain with three ships: the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María. He was looking for a new way to Asia. Instead he reached islands in the Caribbean Sea. After 1492, ships began to cross the ocean again and again, and life changed for the people on both sides.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: Leif Erikson, then Columbus almost 500 years later, then Jamestown.

blocks.html: People sometimes say Columbus "discovered" America. But millions of people already lived here: the first peoples. Columbus's voyage began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas. He thought he had reached the Indies, near Asia, so he called the people he met "Indians."

For the grown-up: Columbus Day is the second Monday in October; many states and cities mark that day as Indigenous Peoples' Day, to honor Native peoples. Contact also brought new diseases that took many Native lives.

blocks.html: After the explorers, people from England came to stay. In 1607, three small ships landed in Virginia. The settlers named their town Jamestown, after their king, James.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Jamestown, in Virginia, and Plymouth, farther north.

blocks.html: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first English settlement in America that lasted.

About 104 men and boys came to Jamestown. Many hoped to find gold and get rich. Instead they found hard times: bad water, sickness and too little food. The land was already home to the Powhatan people, led by a chief called Powhatan. At first the Powhatan traded food with the settlers, which helped them live. Later, the settlers learned to grow tobacco to sell, and the town grew.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Ships, wooden houses and corn traded from the Powhatan.

blocks.html: Some children think the Pilgrims came first. Jamestown came first, in 1607. The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in 1620, thirteen years later.
For the grown-up: Pocahontas, the daughter of Chief Powhatan, is part of Jamestown's story. Relations between the settlers and the Powhatan turned to war more than once as the colony took more land.

sources.name: National Park Service, Historic Jamestowne: "A Short History of Jamestown"
Grokipedia, "Jamestown, Virginia" (founded May 14, 1607)
Grokipedia, "Pocahontas" (daughter of Powhatan)

blocks.html: In 1620, a ship named the Mayflower crossed the ocean from England. On board were about 100 people. Some of them we call the Pilgrims.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Mayflower. The trip took about two months on a crowded ship.

blocks.html: The Pilgrims came mainly to worship God in their own way. They founded Plymouth Colony, and before landing they agreed to make fair laws together.

In England, everyone was supposed to go to the king's church. The Pilgrims wanted their own church, so they left. Before they went ashore, the men on the ship signed the Mayflower Compact. It was a promise to make fair laws for the good of the colony and to obey them. It was an early step toward people governing themselves. Their first winter was very hard, and about half of them died.
Some children think the Pilgrims came to find gold. That was the hope of many Jamestown settlers. The Pilgrims came mainly for their religion, and they came as families, with children.
For the grown-up: The Mayflower left England in September 1620 with 102 passengers. The Compact was signed on November 11, 1620, by 41 men, while the ship lay off Cape Cod.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Mayflower" (102 passengers, 1620)
Grokipedia, "Mayflower Compact" (signed by 41 men, November 11, 1620)
Grokipedia, "Plymouth Colony" (nearly half died the first winter)

blocks.html: The Pilgrims built Plymouth on land of the Wampanoag people. A Wampanoag leader named Massasoit made peace with them.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Corn, wild birds and deer were part of the harvest feast.

blocks.html: In the fall of 1621, the Pilgrims and about 90 Wampanoag men, led by Massasoit, shared a harvest feast that lasted about three days.

A man named Squanto (Tisquantum) had learned English. He showed the Pilgrims how to plant corn and where to fish. Thanks to that help, the Pilgrims had a good harvest. To celebrate, they went hunting for birds. Massasoit and his men came, and they went out and brought back five deer. Everyone ate and celebrated together.

blocks.name: cv-order

items: Squanto shows how to plant corn (spring 1621)

blocks.cap: Put the story in order.

blocks.html: Many pictures show a small dinner with pie. The real feast lasted about three days, and the Wampanoag brought deer. We know about it from a letter written in 1621 by a Pilgrim, Edward Winslow.

For the grown-up: Squanto had been taken to Europe by an English ship captain years before, and there he learned English. When he came home, he found his village, Patuxet, emptied by sickness; Plymouth was built where it had stood.

sources.name: Edward Winslow, letter of December 11, 1621, printed in Mourt's Relation (London, 1622), as given by Plimoth Patuxet Museums
Pilgrim Hall Museum, "The First Thanksgiving" (Winslow's and Bradford's accounts)
Grokipedia, "Squanto" (Tisquantum of the Patuxet)

blocks.html: After Jamestown and Plymouth, more English colonies began. A colony is a place ruled by a faraway country.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: The thirteen colonies, from New Hampshire in the north to Georgia in the south.

blocks.html: By 1732 there were thirteen English colonies along the Atlantic coast. Georgia was the last of the thirteen.

The colonies were in three groups. The New England colonies in the north had rocky soil, fishing and shipbuilding. The Middle colonies grew wheat and had busy port cities. The Southern colonies had warm weather and big farms. Later, these thirteen colonies became the first thirteen states.

blocks.name: cv-flag
blocks.cap: The 13 stripes on our flag stand for the thirteen colonies.

blocks.html: Some children think the colonies covered the whole country. They were a narrow strip along the ocean. Most of the land to the west was still home to Native nations.

For the grown-up: The thirteen: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Find your state, or the nearest colony, on the map.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Thirteen Colonies" (the colonies and their regions)
Grokipedia, "Province of Georgia" (founded 1732)

blocks.html: The thirteen colonies were ruled by Britain and its king, King George III. For a long time, most colonists were happy to be British. Then things changed.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A king's crown, a ship that carried tea, and the three-cornered hat many colonists wore.

blocks.html: Britain's lawmakers, called Parliament, put new taxes on the colonists. The colonists had no vote in Parliament. They said: "No taxation without representation!"

A tax is money people pay to the government. In 1765 Parliament taxed paper, and later it taxed tea. Many colonists said only leaders they had chosen should tax them. In 1773 some colonists in Boston dumped chests of tea from three ships into the harbor: the Boston Tea Party. Britain sent more soldiers, and in 1775 fighting began. The war for independence, the American Revolution, had started.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, from first to last.

blocks.html: Some children think the colonists did not want to pay any taxes. Their complaint was about who decided the taxes. They wanted taxes voted on by leaders they had chosen, not by a Parliament far away where they had no say.
For the grown-up: "Representation" means having someone you chose speak and vote for you. Not every colonist wanted to break away; many, called Loyalists, stayed loyal to the king.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Stamp Act 1765" (the 1765 tax on printed paper)
Grokipedia, "Boston Tea Party" (December 16, 1773: 342 chests of tea)
Grokipedia, "No taxation without representation" (the colonists' argument)

blocks.html: In 1776, leaders from all thirteen colonies met in Philadelphia. They asked Thomas Jefferson to write down why the colonies should be free. He wrote the Declaration of Independence.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Declaration was written with a quill pen. It was adopted in Philadelphia, home of the Liberty Bell.

blocks.html: The Declaration says all men are created equal and have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. It was adopted on July 4, 1776.

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.text: Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness
marks.note: The right to live, to be free and to try to find happiness.

blocks.cap: Famous words from the Declaration. Tap the highlighted words.

blocks.html: The Declaration said that people have rights that no king can take away, and that a government should protect those rights. Because the king had not, the colonies said they would be free and form a new country. Fifty-six leaders signed it. John Hancock wrote his name very big.
Some children think the colonies became free the day the Declaration was signed. The Declaration said they were free. Then they had to win a war, which ended in 1783.

For the grown-up: In 1776 many people, including enslaved people and women, did not have the rights the Declaration named. Over the years, many Americans worked to make its words true for everyone. The document is kept at the National Archives in Washington, D.C.

sources.name: The Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776 (National Archives transcription)
Grokipedia, "United States Declaration of Independence" (drafted by Jefferson; signed by 56 delegates, most on August 2, 1776)

blocks.html: George Washington was born in Virginia in 1732. He was a farmer and a soldier. When the colonies fought for freedom, they chose him to lead their army.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A soldier's three-cornered hat and drum, and the government he helped begin.

blocks.html: Washington led the Continental Army in the Revolution. In 1789 he became our first President. He is called the Father of His Country.

The war was long and hard. One winter, at Valley Forge, the soldiers were cold and hungry, but Washington kept the army together. In 1781 his army won a big victory at Yorktown, and the war soon ended. Then the people chose him as the first President. After two terms, eight years, he stepped down and went home, so that a new leader could be chosen.

Some children think Washington was a king, or was President during the war. He led the army in the war. He became President years later, after the Constitution was written. He was never a king: he chose to give up power.

For the grown-up: Washington enslaved people at his home, Mount Vernon; in his will he ordered that the people he enslaved be freed after his wife's death. The capital, Washington, D.C., is named for him.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "George Washington" (born February 22, 1732; first President 1789 to 1797; his will)

blocks.html: George Washington did not win the Revolution alone. Many people helped, in many different ways.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Lanterns in a church tower warned that British soldiers were coming. Ships brought help from France. Drummers marched with the army.

blocks.html: Paul Revere rode at night to warn that British soldiers were coming. Ben Franklin went to France and won its help. Soldiers, sailors and families of every background served.

On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere rode to warn the towns near Boston. Ben Franklin, a famous writer and inventor, convinced France to send soldiers, ships and money. A young Frenchman, the Marquis de Lafayette, fought beside Washington. About 5,000 Black soldiers served in the American army. Women ran farms and shops while the men were away, and a few, like Deborah Sampson, even dressed as men to join the army.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Rode at night to warn the towns
Was a famous inventor and writer

blocks.cap: Who did what?

blocks.html: Some children think only generals won the war. Farmers, women, Black soldiers and sailors, Native allies and friends from France all played a part. Most were people whose names we do not know.

For the grown-up: Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John in 1776 asking him to "remember the ladies" in the new laws. Some Native nations, like the Oneida, sided with the Americans; others sided with Britain.

blocks.html: After the war, the new country needed a plan for its government. In 1787, leaders met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Constitution, a quill pen, and the Declaration of Independence: two different papers.

blocks.html: The Constitution is our country's rulebook. It says how the government works and what it may and may not do. It begins with the words "We the People."

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.note: The government belongs to the people. The people are the boss.

blocks.cap: The first words of the Constitution, called the Preamble. Tap the first three words.

blocks.html: A team needs rules everyone agrees on. So does a country. George Washington led the meeting, and James Madison shared many of the ideas. They signed the Constitution on September 17, 1787. Later, people added changes called amendments. The first ten, the Bill of Rights, protect freedoms like speaking and worshiping freely. The Constitution still guides the country today.
The Declaration and the Constitution are easy to mix up. The Declaration (1776) said we would be free. The Constitution (1787) set up how our government works.

blocks.name: cv-sort
blocks.cap: Which paper is it?

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Constitution Day is September 17. Thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution, and it now has 27 amendments. Read the Preamble aloud together and talk about one goal in it, such as "establish Justice."

sources.name: The Constitution of the United States, 1787 (National Archives transcription)
Grokipedia, "Constitution of the United States" (signed September 17, 1787, by 39 delegates)
The Bill of Rights, 1791 (National Archives transcription)

blocks.html: The Constitution splits the work of the government into three parts, called branches, like three branches of one tree.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Three branches, three jobs.

blocks.html: Congress makes the laws. The President carries out the laws. The courts decide what the laws mean.

The writers of the Constitution did not want any one person to have all the power, the way a king did. So they gave each branch its own job, and each branch can check the others. Congress works in the Capitol. The President works in the White House. The highest court, the Supreme Court, has nine judges, called justices.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Capitol (Congress), the White House (the President) and a judge's gavel (the courts).

blocks.html: Many children think the President makes all the laws. Congress makes the laws. The President can sign a law or say no to it, and then carries the laws out. The courts settle questions about what the laws mean.
For the grown-up: A memory trick: Congress "makes," the President "does," the courts "decide." The three branches are named in the first three articles of the Constitution.

sources.name: The Constitution of the United States, 1787 (National Archives transcription)
Ben's Guide to the U.S. Government (U.S. Government Publishing Office)
Grokipedia, "Supreme Court of the United States" (nine justices)

blocks.html: In 1803 the United States bought a huge piece of land in the West from France. It was called the Louisiana Purchase, and it made the country about twice as big. But what was out there?

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: The route of Lewis and Clark, from near St. Louis to the Pacific Ocean (simplified).

blocks.html: In 1804, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out to explore the West. Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman, helped them. They reached the Pacific Ocean in 1805.

President Thomas Jefferson asked Lewis and Clark to find a way west by river, draw maps, and learn about the plants, animals and peoples of the land. Their group, the Corps of Discovery, paddled boats up the Missouri River and crossed the Rocky Mountains. Sacagawea spoke Shoshone. When they met her people, her brother was a Shoshone chief, and the Shoshone traded them the horses they needed to cross the mountains. In 1806 the explorers came home.
Some children think Lewis and Clark found empty land. They met many Native nations along the way. Sacagawea and other Native people helped them find routes, food and horses.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Canoes, a compass, and the bison herds the explorers saw on the plains.

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Sacagawea made the trip while caring for her baby son, Jean Baptiste. The explorers kept journals, so we can still read what they saw. The trip followed Washington's time by only a few years.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Lewis and Clark Expedition" (the Corps of Discovery, 1804 to 1806)
Grokipedia, "Sacagawea" (Lemhi Shoshone; her brother Cameahwait; horses for the mountains)
Grokipedia, "Louisiana Purchase" (1803; it about doubled the country's size)

blocks.html: After Lewis and Clark, many families wanted new land in the West. They were called pioneers. In the 1840s, thousands set out on the Oregon Trail.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 miles, from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon City.

blocks.html: Pioneers packed covered wagons, pulled by oxen, and traveled west. The trip took five or six months.

A wagon was the family's moving truck. It was packed full of flour, bacon, tools, pots and clothes, so there was little room to ride. Oxen pulled it slowly, mile after mile. The pioneers crossed rivers, plains and mountains. At night they circled the wagons and cooked over a fire. Later, people rushed to California to look for gold, and in 1869 a railroad made the trip much faster.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A covered wagon, a log cabin to build at the end, and the train that came later.

blocks.html: Some children picture pioneers riding in the wagon the whole way. Most of them walked beside the wagon, which was packed full. Children walked too, and helped with chores.

For the grown-up: Native nations lived along the trails. Many traded food and guided travelers across rivers; as more and more settlers came and took land, there was also conflict. Between 1840 and 1869, over 500,000 people went west.

sources.name: National Park Service, Oregon National Historic Trail Junior Ranger book (2020): most walked beside their wagons; the trip took 5 or 6 months
National Park Service, Oregon National Historic Trail brochure: a 2,000-mile route; over 500,000 pioneers went west between 1840 and 1869
Grokipedia, "Oregon Trail" (from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon City)

blocks.html: This is a hard part of our country's story, and it is important to know. For a long time, many people in America were enslaved.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A broken chain stands for the end of slavery.

blocks.html: People who were enslaved were not free. They were forced to work without pay, and they could not choose where to live. Slavery in the United States ended in 1865.

Starting in the 1600s, people were taken from their homes in Africa and brought across the ocean on ships. They and their children were enslaved. They worked on farms and in homes and towns, in all thirteen colonies. Enslaved people kept their families, songs and faith as best they could, and many tried to escape. After the Revolution, the Northern states began to end slavery, but in the South it grew. It took a long struggle and the Civil War to end slavery everywhere, in 1865.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: From 1619 to 1865 is more than 200 years.

blocks.html: Some children think slavery was only in one place, or that it ended as soon as people said it was wrong. It was in all thirteen colonies, and it lasted more than 200 years. Many people, enslaved and free, worked for a long time to end it.

For the grown-up: Children may feel sad or upset. Let them ask questions and answer simply. The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) ended slavery in the United States; Juneteenth remembers the news of freedom reaching Texas.

sources.name: U.S. Constitution, Thirteenth Amendment, 1865 (National Archives transcription)
Grokipedia, "Slavery in the United States" (the first recorded Africans in Virginia, 1619, to the Thirteenth Amendment, 1865)
OpenStax U.S. History, Section 3.4 and Chapter 15 (book and section; no URL)

blocks.html: Some brave people escaped from slavery and then helped others become free. Two of the most famous are Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: People escaping at night followed the North Star. Douglass wrote with a pen.

blocks.html: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and led others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. Frederick Douglass escaped and became a great speaker and writer against slavery.

Harriet Tubman was enslaved in Maryland. In 1849 she escaped to Philadelphia, where she was free. Then she went back, again and again, about 13 times, and led about 70 people to freedom. Frederick Douglass escaped in 1838. As a boy he had learned to read in secret. He wrote books, started a newspaper and gave speeches that changed many minds.

The Underground Railroad was not a real train under the ground! It was a secret network of people and hiding places, such as homes and barns, that helped people escape to freedom. Helpers were called "conductors," like on a train.

blocks.name: cv-sort
blocks.cap: Who did what?

blocks.html: For the grown-up: Tubman later served the Union Army in the Civil War as a scout and nurse. Douglass met with President Lincoln. You may hear bigger numbers for Tubman; the National Park Service says about 70 people in about 13 trips.

sources.name: National Park Service, Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park: "Myths and Facts" (about 70 people in about 13 trips)
Grokipedia, "Harriet Tubman" (escaped September 1849)
Grokipedia, "Frederick Douglass" (escaped September 1838; Narrative, 1845; The North Star)

blocks.html: Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a small log cabin in Kentucky. He loved to read and taught himself many things. He grew up to be a lawyer, and people called him "Honest Abe."

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A log cabin like the one where Lincoln was born, his tall stovepipe hat, and a broken chain for freedom.

blocks.html: Lincoln was the 16th President. He led the country through the Civil War (1861 to 1865), worked to end slavery and kept the country together.

When Lincoln was elected, many states in the South left the country because they wanted to keep slavery. The North and the South fought the Civil War. In 1863 Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, which said enslaved people in the rebelling states were free. That same year he gave a short, famous speech at Gettysburg. The North won in 1865, the country stayed one, and slavery ended. Lincoln died in April 1865, just after the war.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: Lincoln became President more than 70 years after Washington.

blocks.html: Some children think Lincoln was the first President, or lived at the same time as Washington. Washington was the 1st President (1789). Lincoln was the 16th (1861), more than 70 years later.

For the grown-up: Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865, and died the next day; share that when your child is ready. His face is on the five-dollar bill, and the Lincoln Memorial stands in Washington, D.C.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Abraham Lincoln" (born February 12, 1809, in a Kentucky log cabin; the 16th President)
Abraham Lincoln, the Gettysburg Address, November 19, 1863 (the Bliss copy, Library of Congress)

blocks.html: An inventor makes something new that people have never had before. American inventors changed how we live, work and travel.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: Franklin's kite, an early telephone, a light bulb and the Wright brothers' airplane.

blocks.html: Ben Franklin showed that lightning is electricity (1752). Alexander Graham Bell made the telephone (1876). Thomas Edison made a light bulb that lasted (1879). The Wright brothers flew the first airplane (1903).

Each invention solved a problem. Franklin's discovery led to the lightning rod, which protects buildings. The telephone let people talk across long distances. Edison's bulb lit homes after dark without a flame. On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew for 12 seconds, the first powered airplane flight a person controlled. Today we fly all over the world.

It is easy to mix up who made what. Also, inventors seldom work alone: Edison had a whole team in his laboratory, and the Wright brothers were two brothers working together. Match each invention to its inventor and its year.
For the grown-up: Look around your home for inventions: the light switch, the phone, a fan. Ask, "What did people do before this was invented?"

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Benjamin Franklin" (the 1752 kite experiment and the lightning rod)
Grokipedia, "Alexander Graham Bell" (first telephone call, March 10, 1876)

blocks.html: Our country began with thirteen states along the Atlantic. As pioneers moved west, new states joined, one at a time.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Slide through the years and watch the states join.

blocks.html: Today there are 50 states. The first was Delaware, in 1787. The last two, Alaska and Hawaii, joined in 1959.

When enough people lived in a new place, they could ask Congress to let them become a state. Each state has its own government and its own capital city, where its leaders work. Texas's capital is Austin, and California's is Sacramento. When a new state joined, a new star went on the flag.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Each square is a state, colored by when it joined.

blocks.html: Some children think all 50 states joined at once, or that Alaska and Hawaii were first because they are on the edge of the map. States joined one at a time, from 1787 to 1959. Alaska and Hawaii were the last.
For the grown-up: Find your state on the tile map. When did it join, and what is its capital? Alaska is the largest state; Hawaii is made of islands in the Pacific Ocean.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Admission to the Union" (Delaware first, December 7, 1787; Alaska January 3, 1959; Hawaii August 21, 1959)

blocks.html: Clara Barton was born in Massachusetts in 1821. She began her work as a teacher. When the Civil War came, in Lincoln's time, she found a new way to help.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: The Red Cross, helping hands, and the wagons Clara Barton used to bring supplies.

blocks.html: Clara Barton cared for wounded soldiers in the Civil War. In 1881 she started the American Red Cross, which still helps people after disasters.

During the war, Clara Barton brought food, bandages and comfort right to the battlefields, where soldiers needed help most. A doctor called her an "angel of the battlefield." After the war she helped families find soldiers who were missing. Then she started the American Red Cross. Today, when there is a flood, a fire or a storm, Red Cross volunteers bring shelter, food and blankets.

Some children think helpers are only people in uniforms today. People have served others all through history, and many of them were volunteers, people who help without being paid. Clara Barton did much of her work as a volunteer.
For the grown-up: Clara Barton led the American Red Cross for 23 years. Talk about ways your family can volunteer, as community helpers do.

sources.name: National Park Service, "Clara Barton"
Grokipedia, "Clara Barton" (founded the American Red Cross on May 21, 1881)

blocks.html: About a hundred years after Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass, many people were still not treated fairly. In some places, unfair laws kept people apart by race: in schools, at lunch counters and on buses.

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A city bus in Montgomery, Alabama, became part of history.

blocks.html: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks would not give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. helped lead a bus boycott and peaceful marches for equal treatment.

The law in Montgomery said Black riders had to give up their seats when the driver told them to. Rosa Parks said no, and she was arrested. To protest, people stopped riding the buses. They walked or shared rides for more than a year. That is a boycott. In 1956 the Supreme Court said the bus law was unfair and against the Constitution. Dr. King became a leader of peaceful protests all over the country.
Some people say Rosa Parks was just tired that day. She said the only tired she was, was tired of giving in. She had worked for fair treatment for years.

For the grown-up: Rosa Parks worked for the NAACP in Montgomery for years before 1955. In 1963 Dr. King spoke at the March on Washington, to about 250,000 people at the Lincoln Memorial. See also Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Rosa Parks" (December 1, 1955; "tired of giving in," from her autobiography Rosa Parks: My Story (1992))
Grokipedia, "Montgomery bus boycott" (December 5, 1955, to December 20, 1956; Browder v. Gayle)
Grokipedia, "I Have a Dream" (August 28, 1963, at the Lincoln Memorial)

blocks.html: For thousands of years, people looked up at the Moon and wondered what it was like. In 1969, American astronauts went there!

blocks.name: cv-picture
blocks.cap: A rocket, and the American flag on the Moon.

blocks.html: On July 20, 1969, astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon. Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.

The trip was called Apollo 11. A giant rocket, the Saturn V, carried three astronauts into space. Michael Collins flew around the Moon in their ship, Columbia, while Armstrong and Aldrin went down in a small lander called the Eagle. As he stepped onto the Moon, Armstrong said it was "one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind." They planted a flag, collected Moon rocks and came safely home.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: Only 66 years passed between the first airplane flight and the Moon landing.

blocks.html: Some children think astronauts flew to the Moon in an airplane. Airplanes need air, and there is no air in space. The astronauts rode a huge rocket, and they landed in the Eagle.

For the grown-up: Thousands of people worked on Apollo: engineers, scientists, mathematicians and builders. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. Look at the Moon together tonight.

sources.name: NASA, "Apollo 11 Mission Overview"
Grokipedia, "Apollo 11" (crew, Eagle and Columbia)

blocks.html: You have learned a lot of American history! Now let's put the big events in order, from long ago to not so long ago.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: A time line puts events in order and shows how far apart they were.

blocks.html: A time line shows events in order, from the oldest to the newest. A bigger number year came later.

blocks.title: Who came first?
blocks.q: Put these in order: Abraham Lincoln, Dr. King, George Washington.
steps: Find each year: Washington became President in 1789. Lincoln became President in 1861. Dr. King gave his famous speech in 1963.
The smallest year is the oldest: 1789, then 1861, then 1963.
The order is Washington, Lincoln, King. About 70 years passed from Washington to Lincoln, and about 100 more to Dr. King.

blocks.html: Life long ago was different. To light the night, people used candles and lanterns; now we have light bulbs. People traveled by wagon and sailing ship; now we have cars and airplanes. To talk to someone far away, people wrote letters; now we can call on a phone. Some things stay the same: families, helping each other, and our flag.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put these in order, oldest first.

blocks.html: Some children put Washington, Lincoln and Dr. King all "a long time ago," at the same time. A time line shows they lived far apart. Washington and Dr. King lived almost 200 years apart.

For the grown-up: Make a family time line: when grandparents were born, when your child was born, when they started school. Then put a few events from this course on it. Review the 1621 harvest and Fifty States.
